topics.title: The interview: an art or an intrusion?

learn.hook: Every evening, news channels run interviews with cricketers, ministers and film stars. Yet until the mid-1800s, the interview did not even exist as a form of journalism.
points: Part I: Christopher Silvester's introduction to 'The Penguin Book of Interviews', on the history of interviews and views about them.
Part II: an extract from Mukund Padmanabhan's interview with the Italian writer Umberto Eco, published in The Hindu.
The interview was invented a little over 130 years before Silvester wrote, and has become a commonplace of journalism.
Positive view: at its best the interview is a source of truth and, in practice, an art; the interviewer holds great power and influence.
Negative view: an unwarranted intrusion into private lives that diminishes the celebrities interviewed.

example.q: Why is the interview described as a 'commonplace of journalism'?
steps: Commonplace means ordinary and very common.
Today interviews appear daily in newspapers, TV and online.
So, though it was invented only about 130 years earlier, it is now everywhere.
example.answer: Because interviews have become so common in the media that almost everyone has read or seen one.

learn.reallife: From post-match interviews at the IPL to budget-day interviews with the Finance Minister, the interview is a routine part of Indian media today.

quiz.explain: The interviewer occupies a position of unprecedented power and influence.

options: It is a reliable source of truth

teach.praise: Great interview skills! Some see it as an art and a source of truth; others as an intrusion that diminishes people.
teach.nudge: Give me one positive and one negative view.

learn.hook: One of the world's most loved children's writers refused every interviewer who knocked. He had his reasons.
points: Some primitive cultures believe a photograph steals a person's soul; similarly, V.S. Naipaul felt that some people are wounded by interviews and lose a part of themselves.
Lewis Carroll, author of 'Alice in Wonderland', had a 'defensive dread' of interviewers and never consented to be interviewed; he hated being lionised.
Rudyard Kipling called the interview immoral, a crime, an offence against his person, an assault that deserved punishment, and cowardly and vile.
Kipling's wife wrote in her diary that their day was 'wrecked by two reporters from Boston'.

example.q: What is the link between the 'photograph steals the soul' belief and Naipaul's view?
steps: The belief: a camera takes away part of a person's spirit.
Naipaul: an interview takes away part of the person interviewed.
Both see a loss of self in being recorded.
example.answer: Both suggest that being photographed or interviewed takes away a part of a person's self.

learn.reallife: Some Indian sportspeople avoid media before big events. Like Carroll, they feel constant attention takes something away from them.

topics.title: Wells, Bellow, Brian and the power of the interviewer

learn.hook: Imagine thumbprints pressing on your throat. That is how one Nobel-winning novelist described being interviewed.
points: H.G. Wells called it 'the ordeal of the interview', yet he was interviewed often and later himself interviewed Joseph Stalin.
Saul Bellow agreed to interviews many times but described them as 'thumbprints on his windpipe', a feeling of being choked.
Denis Brian wrote that today we learn most about our contemporaries through interviews.
Theme: interviews are both an art and an intrusion; the interviewer holds great power to shape how the public sees a person.

example.q: Explain the metaphor 'thumbprints on his windpipe'.
steps: The windpipe carries air; pressure on it means choking.
Interviews made Bellow feel suffocated and pressed.
So the metaphor shows extreme discomfort.
example.answer: Interviews made Bellow feel as if he were being choked; they were suffocating and painful.

learn.reallife: A single TV interview can change a public figure's image overnight in India. That is the 'power and influence' of the interviewer Silvester describes.

quiz.explain: Both true; shaping public image is the source of that power.

quiz.explain: A is false: he consented several times. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Assumes disliking interviews means refusing them all

learn.hook: A professor of 'signs' writes a medieval murder mystery that sells millions of copies. Meet Umberto Eco.
points: Umberto Eco: an Italian professor of semiotics, the study of signs and symbols, at the University of Bologna.
His work spans scholarly books on semiotics, literary interpretation and medieval aesthetics, plus essays and novels.
His novel 'The Name of the Rose' (1980), a medieval detective story, sold between 10 and 15 million copies.
He calls himself a university professor who writes novels on Sundays: he sees himself first as an academic.

example.q: What does Eco mean when he says he writes novels 'on Sundays'?
steps: His main identity is academic: a professor of semiotics.
Novels are something he does in his spare time.
So he means novel-writing is a side activity.
example.answer: He sees himself mainly as a scholar; novel-writing is a weekend or spare-time pursuit.

learn.reallife: Many Indian professionals write novels on the side: doctors, IAS officers and bankers. Like Eco, their 'Sunday' writing sometimes becomes a bestseller.

learn.hook: How does one man write scholarly books, essays, a newspaper column and bestselling novels? He uses the gaps.
points: Eco works in 'interstices', the small empty spaces of time between tasks, such as waiting for a lift to arrive.
He says that if all the empty space were removed from the universe's atoms, the universe would be as small as his fist; likewise, our lives are full of empty spaces we can use.
His scholarly writing uses a playful, personal, narrative style, telling the story of his research instead of being dry and formal.
Theme: creativity and the efficient use of time.
Metaphor: 'interstices', literally tiny gaps between things, is used for the small gaps in a day.

example.q: Give an example of using 'interstices' in a student's day.
steps: Find a small gap: the 10-minute bus ride to school.
Use it for a small task: revising formula cards or new words.
Many such gaps add up to hours of work.
example.answer: Revising flashcards during a short bus ride or while waiting for class is using interstices.

learn.reallife: Students revising on the Mumbai local or the Delhi Metro are using Eco's interstices. Ten minutes twice a day adds up to over 100 hours in a year.

topics.title: Why did The Name of the Rose succeed?

learn.hook: A difficult novel full of medieval history and theology became a global bestseller. Even its author called this a mystery.
points: Eco thinks the novel's success is a mystery; he says it might not have sold if written ten years earlier or ten years later.
The novel is serious and demanding, a detective story that goes into metaphysics, theology and medieval history, yet it found a mass audience.
Eco suggests readers do not only want easy reading; many enjoy serious, challenging books, and the medieval setting attracted them.
Theme: popularity, scholarship and fiction can meet; a scholar can be a bestselling novelist.
Form: Part I is expository prose packed with quotations; Part II follows a question-answer interview format.

example.q: How does Eco explain the success of 'The Name of the Rose'?
steps: He calls it a mystery that depended on timing.
Readers were drawn by its medieval setting and serious content.
He rejects the idea that readers only want easy books.
example.answer: He says it is a mystery linked to timing; readers enjoyed its serious content and medieval setting, though it was not easy reading.

learn.reallife: Indian bestsellers on mythology and history show the same thing Eco noticed: readers will take on serious, layered stories when the setting fascinates them.

learn.hook: 'Who is lionised today?' Answer that, and you'll see why writers like Carroll ran from reporters.
points: Positive views: art, source of truth, a way to know contemporaries. Negative views: intrusion, diminishing, wounding, a crime. Celebrity writers dislike interviews because they intrude and take something away.
The photograph belief: primitive cultures fear a picture steals the soul; 'thumbprints on his windpipe' means a choking, suffocating feeling.
To be lionised is to be treated as a celebrity. Today film stars, sports stars and influencers are lionised because of media attention.
Eco's interstices explain his output; his academic writing is personal and playful because he tells research as a story.
Eco on his novel's success: a mystery of timing; readers liked its serious content and medieval setting.

example.q: Who is lionised today, and why?
steps: Lionise = treat as a celebrity.
Examples: cricketers, film stars, social media influencers.
Reason: constant media coverage and public admiration.
example.answer: Cricketers, film stars and influencers are lionised today because the media covers them constantly and fans admire them.

learn.reallife: When an Indian athlete wins Olympic gold, crowds, interviews and ads follow within hours. That is lionising, and Carroll's 'horror' of it makes more sense.

topics.title: Conducting an interview and exam answers

learn.hook: Your school magazine wants an interview with the principal. You have 15 minutes. What do you ask?
points: The interview as journalism: it informs, reveals personality and shapes opinion, but must respect privacy and consent.
Planning an interview: research the person, prepare open questions (what, why, how), start easy, then go deeper, and listen and follow up.
Conducting it: take permission to record, be polite, note exact words, check facts before publishing.
Short answers: views on interviews (positive and negative) and Eco's interstices. Long answer: the interview as a medium, its power, art and risks.

example.q: Plan three good opening questions for an interview with a local doctor.
steps: Begin with an easy, open question.
Move to their work and challenges.
End with advice for students.
example.answer: What made you choose medicine? What is a typical day like at your clinic? What advice would you give students who want to become doctors?

learn.reallife: Podcasts by Indian entrepreneurs and sportspeople show interviews at their best: well-researched questions, real listening and respect for the guest.

quiz.explain: A balanced answer covers both positive and negative views.

quiz.explain: Using small gaps of time is a key point about Eco.
